tagline: From a White Mountains watershed divide to the Saco valley
intro: Pequawket Trail Scenic Byway links the Saco River valley with Route 113’s passage through Evans Notch in the White Mountains. Maine designated the state byway in 2007, from Route 25 in Standish to the Batchelders Grant/Gilead town line. The National Scenic Byway Foundation highlights working farms, historic villages and wildlife habitats along the drive. In the north, Route 113 follows the state border and crosses into and out of New Hampshire twice.

The older Pequawket Trail ran between Standish and Fryeburg, and Hiram became a stage stop along it. Route 113 received its number in 1925 and initially ended at Fryeburg. The extension to Gilead came in 1937. A realignment at Stow in 1940–41 left an older loop that became New Hampshire Route 113B.

Following the byway south from the Gilead town line brings Evans Notch first, then Fryeburg on the Saco. The pass lies between the Royce Mountains to the west and Speckled Mountain to the east. Beyond Fryeburg, the journey continues through Brownfield and Hiram toward Steep Falls. There, Route 113 shares the road with Route 11 before continuing southeast toward Standish and its junction with Route 25.

moments.title: Evans Notch
moments.text: Water on either side of Evans Notch takes different routes to the coast. The 1,410-foot pass is the easternmost notch through the White Mountains. Southward drainage reaches the Saco through the Cold and Charles rivers; northward drainage reaches the Androscoggin through Evans Brook and the Wild River. Route 113 crosses this divide between the Royce Mountains on the west and Speckled Mountain on the east. West Royce’s summit lies in New Hampshire, while East Royce stands in Maine. The Saco reaches the Gulf of Maine at Saco and Biddeford; the Androscoggin joins the Kennebec at Merrymeeting Bay.

moments.title: Jockey Cap, Fryeburg
moments.text: A bronze profile of the surrounding hills turns Jockey Cap’s summit into a landscape guide. Arctic explorer Robert Peary lived in Fryeburg in 1878–79 and surveyed the hills and mountains visible from this granite glacial erratic beside the Saco River. His boyhood friend Alfred E. Burton proposed making that survey into a monument. In 1938, the Peary family dedicated the resulting monument to his memory, setting a bronze cast of the profile survey on a cylinder of granite. A half-mile hiking trail leads to the rock’s summit and the memorial.
moments.notice: The bronze survey rests on a granite cylinder at the summit.

moments.title: Hiram
moments.text: Hiram’s stage-stop history became a railroad-junction story. The town served travelers on the Pequawket Trail between Standish and Fryeburg, then connected the Bridgton and Saco River Railroad with the Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad. Water also put Hiram to work: the Saco and tributary streams powered mills, and timber manufacturing became an important industry. By 1886, five sawmills and planing mills produced lumber and barrel components. The town is drained by both the Saco and Ossipee rivers. Its earlier name, Great Ossipee, came from the Ossipee River, one of the waterways that shaped this mill town.
